3.2. Sample and measure of economic dependence
Prior rcscarch indicatcs that Big Fivc firms havc a rcputation advantagc ovcr
non-Big Five firms, and that the incentives of companies choosing non-Big
Five auditors are different from those audited by the Big Five firms (Craswell
et al., 1995; Francis and Wilson, 1988). For this reason our study is restricted
to companies audited by the more homogeneous group of Big Five accounting
firms. The term Big Five is used for convenience even though data in the study
predate the 1998 merger that created Pricewaterhousecoopers which reduced
the then Big Six group of leading accounting firms to the Big Five..
The accruals sample is comprised of 6,747 U.S. companies having Big Five
auditors for fiscal 1996 as reported in Compact Disclosure dated October 1997.
For each of these observations, the local office of the Big Five accounting firm
with primary engagement responsibility is identified from the signed audit
report. The audit report is obtained from 10-K filings in the SEC's EDGAR
archives. A total of 499 local offices of Big Five accounting firms conducted
audits of the 6,747 companies in the sample. These 499 offices have an average
of 13.5 publicly-listed clients per office, and a range of 1-139 clients per office.
The variable for economic dependence is termed INFLUENCE and is
measured as the size of a client relative to the size of the auditor's office. For
each observation in the sample, INFLUENCE is calculated as the
observation's sales (in natural log form) divided by the sum of sales (in
natural log form) of each publicly-listed company audited by the office. The
rationale for using the natural log of sales is its high correlation with audit fees

382J.K. Reynolds, J.R. Francis / Journal of Accounting and Economics 30 (2001) 375-400
(Craswell et al., 1995; Francis, 1984). The economic importance of a client is
directly proportional to the magnitude of its fees relative to total fees of the
office. INFLUENCE is thus a proxy for the percentage of fees generated by a
client relative to the total for the office that contracts for the engagement,
administers the audit, and issues the audit report.5
3.3. Model specification
Two measures of accounting accruals are used to test hypotheses H1 and H2,
the absolute value of total accruals, and the absolute value of discretionary
accruals. Total accruals are defined as operating net income minus cash flows
from operations, scaled by lagged total assets. The second measure is the.
absolute value of discretionary accruals, scaled by lagged total assets.
Discretionary accruals, denoted DAi, for firm i in industry j for year t, are
computed using the cross-sectional industry variation of Jones' (1991) model
(see DeFond and Jiambalvo, 1994; DeFond and Subramanyam, 1998).
Industry is defined by two-digit SiC code. Discretionary accruals are measured
as the difference between total accruals and non-discretionary accruals. Nondiscretionary (expected) accruals are estimated using a two-step process. First,
the following model is estimated for the full sample by regressing total accruals
on the change in revenues from the prior year and the level of property plant
and equipment to control for the economic determinants of expected accruals:

expected accruals. Discretionary accruals (DA) are then measured as the
absolute value of total accruals (TA) minus the calculated value for nondiscretionary accruals, scaled by lagged total assets.
Previous research identifies several additional factors that may influence the
magnitude of discretionary accruals. The most important of these are operating
cash flows, absolute company size, and leverage (Becker et al., 1998). Operating
cash flows (OCF) are defined as cash flows from operations scaled by lagged
total assets and have been shown to vary inversely with discretionary accruals
(Dechow et al., 1995). Company size is measured as log of sales (SALES) and
may be correlated with operating characteristics that cause large companies to
have systematically smaller accruals, even though accruals are scaled by lagged
assets. Companies with higher debt levels have a greater incentive to use
accruals to increase earnings due to closeness to debt covenant constraints
(DeFond and Jiambalvo, 1994).Debt level (DEBT) is defined as the ratio of
total debt to total assets. Similarly, financially distressed companies also have
an incentive to use accruals to increase earnings. Financial distress is measured
with the Altman Z-score (see PBANK in Table 1). PBANK is expected to be
ncgativcly associated with accruals bccausc a lowcr Z-scorc indicatcs grcatcr
financial distress.

3.4. Results
The initial sample to test H1 and H2 is the 6,747 companies described in
Section 3.2. Companies with missing data needed to estimate the accruals
models are eliminated. In addition, companies in industries with less than five
observations are omitted because of the sensitivity of the cross-sectional
discretionary accruals model to small observations. These screens yield a final
sample of 4952 companies and descriptive statistics are reported in Table 1.
